desc:
Consider strings of length n built only from the first m lowercase letters (a, b, ... in alphabet order). A string is sorted if every character is less than or equal to the character after it, for example "aabc".

Return the number of sorted strings of length n, modulo 1,000,000,007.

n = 2, m = 3  ->  6   (aa, ab, ac, bb, bc, cc)
n = 3, m = 2  ->  4   (aaa, aab, abb, bbb)
hints: Count the strings by their last character: how many sorted strings of length i end in the letter c?
A sorted string of length i ending in c is a sorted string of length i - 1 ending in any letter ≤ c, followed by c.
That sum over letters ≤ c is a prefix sum of the previous row, so each row is computed in O(m). (There is also a closed form with a binomial coefficient.)
editorial: Let dp[c] be the number of sorted strings of the current length that end with letter c. For length 1 every letter works, so all entries are 1. To extend to the next length, a string may end in c if the previous character was any letter up to c, so the new dp[c] is the sum of the old dp[0..c], a running prefix sum. After n - 1 such rounds, the answer is the sum of all entries.

This takes O(n · m) time and O(m) space. A sorted string is fully described by how many times each letter occurs, so the answer is also the number of ways to split n into m non-negative counts, which is the binomial coefficient C(n + m - 1, m - 1) (stars and bars); the DP is the safe way to compute it modulo a prime without modular inverses.
